title: Cu/Cu2O Nanoparticles Supported on Vertically ZIF-L Coated Nitro-gen- Doped Graphene Nanosheets for Electroreduction of CO2 to Ethanol
abstract: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)-derived nanomaterials provide outstanding catalytic activities for CO2 electroreduction due to their large surface area, tunable geometric structures and controllable pore size. Herein, we develop a Cu/ Cu2O nanocomposite loaded on the surface of carbon derived from direct carbonization of two-dimensional cross-like zeolitic imidazolate framework-L coated vertically on graphene oxide (Cu GNC-VL). The as-synthesized catalyst presented an excellent faradaic efficiency (FE) of 70.52 % and current density of 10.4 mA cm−2 at -0.87 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, which benefits from the synergy between CO2 asymmetric chemical adsorption on Cu (111) and favorable kinetics and thermodynamics of C-C coupling on Cu2O (111). This study could present a strategy for the rational design and multi-pathway modulation of geometry structure of MOF-derived catalysts.

sections.heading: Cu/Cu2O Nanoparticles Supported on Vertically ZIF-L Coated Nitrogen-Doped Graphene Nanosheets for Electroreduction of CO2 to Ethanol
sections.text:
Yangyang Zhang a, Kai Li a, Miaomiao Chen a, Jing Wang a, Jindun Liu a, Yatao Zhang a, b * a College of Chemical Engineering, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou 450001, P. R. China b Engineering Research Center of Advanced Manufacturing of Ministry of Education, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou 450001, China ABSTRACT: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)-derived nanomaterials provide outstanding catalytic activities for CO2 electroreduction due to their large surface area, tunable geometric structures and controllable pore size. Herein, we develop a Cu/ Cu2O nanocomposite loaded on the surface of carbon derived from direct carbonization of two-dimensional cross-like zeolitic imidazolate framework-L coated vertically on graphene oxide (Cu GNC-VL). The as-synthesized catalyst presented an excellent faradaic efficiency (FE) of 70.52 % and current density of 10.4 mA cm−2 at -0.87 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, which benefits from the synergy between CO2 asymmetric chemical adsorption on Cu (111) and favorable kinetics and thermodynamics of C-C coupling on Cu2O (111). This study could present a strategy for the rational design and multi-pathway modulation of geometry structure of MOF-derived catalysts.
Keywords: Cu/Cu2O Nanoparticles; Vertically ZIF-L; Nitrogen-Doped Graphene Nanosheets; CO2 Electroreduction; Synergistic Effect
 INTRODUCTION
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to fossil fuels or high-valueadded chemicals has grown into a promising research topic passed through several dozen years development because it provides a cost-effective and sustainable pathway to deal with this greenhouse gas.1-3 Among the various reduction products, C2 hydrocarbons and oxygenates are highly energy-efficiency owing to their high energy densities and demand.4-6 C2H5OH, as a substitute for automotive fuel, is also developed into a potential alternative for conventional batteries.7-9 Nevertheless, the systematic work on various intermediates in CO2 Reduction Reaction (CO2RR) to hydrocarbons by Koper and co-workers demonstrates that the dimerization of *CO is the rate-determining step (RDS) for C2 formation with a more positive onset potential shift, further proving that *CO dimerization may occur.10, 11 Especially, Cu-based catalysts are deemed the most likely ones that can directly reduce CO2 to hydrocarbons and alcohols by the intensive C−C coupling. 8, 12, 13 14, 15 The theoretical evidence of CO dimerization mechanism shows that Cu-based catalysts decrease sharply the thermodynamic and kinetic energy of CO dimerization for enhancing the electroreduction of CO2 to C2 products.4, 16-19 However, most of these Cu-based catalysts still exhibit low selectivity and faraday efficiency for alcohols production in aqueous solution due to the various lattice planes, defects or vacancies of polycrystalline and oxidized Cu.20 Hence, product selectivity of Cu-based catalysts is mainly determined
by adjusting the oxidation states, vacancies, geometric structure, and morphologies.16, 19, 21-24
It is worth noting that crystalline Cu-based catalysts are sought enthusiastically by many researchers, but the amorphous ones with abundant defects and more active sites are in silence. 25-27 Among the various potential amorphous materials, MOFs as kinds of hybrid crystalline are also attractive because of their high specific surface areas and increased catalytic active sites in gas adsorption and separation, molecular catalysis. 28-30 In addition, amorphous Cu derived from carbonization of MOFs affects the catalyst structure, weakening the van der Waals’ interaction between the ligands to generate abundant active sites and increasing the band gap for enhanced semi-conductivity.31, 32 As catalyst candidates, their open channel ensures the adsorption of carbon dioxide molecules in the pore and the diffusion of reduction products along with tunable channel with minimized mass-transfer resistance.33, 34 Nevertheless, a realistic problem is that porous MOFs usually act as electrical insulators. Therefore, MOFs are often compounded with other nanosemiconductor materials such as graphene oxide (GO) and carbon nanotubes (CNTs) to increase the conductivity and facilitate electron-transfer of CO2RR.35-39 In addition, postcarbonization treatment of MOFs derived graphene-based Ndoped porous carbon nanocomposites (GNPCNs) is needed to increase the electrochemical performance of CO2.38, 40-42 However, directly carbonized MOFs will result in breakdown of the open framework structure of MOFs because of their

thermal instability, and cannot construct a continuous conductive medium. Consequently, the reaction mechanism of CO2 electroreduction is so hard to keep integrated at complicated three-phase interface (solid-liquid-gas) on heterogeneous catalyst that the rational design of geometric structure of catalyst occupied an important position.34, 42 Naturally, anchoring MOFs on GO converted to GNPCNs by calcination could be a promotional alternative to exert the synergistic effect between MOF derived N-doped porous carbon (NPC) and GO-derived graphene in CO2 electroreduction because MOFs undergone postcarbonization treatment are transformed into amorphous carbonaceous materials with a large of low-coordinated atoms.43-46 The development of a facile and effective strategy for the preparation of dispersive GO/MOF nanosheets with a uniform and complete MOF coating toward efficient Cu/Cu2O-loaded GNPCNs precursors is repeated for several times.47, 48 But two-dimensional oriented GO/MOF nanocomposites for the CO2 electroreduction has seldom been studied.
ZIF-L, two-dimensional pseudopolymorph of ZIF-8, has widely used in gas separation and sensing, dye adsorption, energy storage due to its regular porous structure, chemical and thermal stability. 49-51 In this work, we prepared oriented ZIF-L derived GO nanosheets by vertical growth of ZIF-L on GO (vZIF-L@GO), introducing copper precursor into above mesoporous supporting layer followed by carbonization at 1000 ℃ for 2h. The as-prepared Cu GNC-VL catalyst built a three-dimensional geometric structure that furnished abundant active site and efficient electronic conductivity. Cu GNC-VL achieved high FEethanol of 70.52% at the total current density of 10.4 mA cm-2 in 0.5 M KHCO3 solution. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that the development of a simple and effective methodology for preparing Cu GNC-VL nanocomposites with a uniform and oriented MOF coating toward efficient CO2RR is worthy to explore.
 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
The leaf-shaped ZIF-L, 2D topology containing large zerodimensional cavities with dimensions of 9.4 Å × 7.0 Å × 5.3 Å (Figure S1a), is constructed of the identical building blocks of ZIF-8 Hmim linkers and Zn2+ ions in deionized water at room temperature.50 it exhibits a uniform flake-like and intergrown crystallites with an average size of 300 nm (Figure S4a). The ZIF-L within flake-like in the ac plane presents six-membered rings comprised of tetrahedral Zn2+ clusters and Hmim linkers (Figure S2), and each Zn atom adopts a regular [ZnN4] tetrahedral geometry. In addition, the 2D network is further stabilize by the interdigitating interactions with the help of the terminal Hmim ligands.50 The hydrogen bond existed in between adjacent Hmim and a weak interaction of the neighbouring layers confirms that the vertical GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites were successfully synthesized by simple synthesis methods. It not only benefits from the mutual support between the cross-like ZIF-L crystallites but also relies on the chelation of Zn ions with oxygen-containing functional groups (OCFGs) of GO, including carboxyl, epoxide, carbonyl and hydroxyl groups.52
The X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure S1b) showed the complete crystal pattern of ZIF-L and GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites, indicating the successful growth of ZIF-L on
GO surface and special vertical distribution of complete vZIFL@GO crystal. This was also supported by the scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of ZIF-L@GO (Figure S4b) and vZIF-L@GO (Figure 1b, c). The 633 nm excited Raman spectra (Figure S3a) of ZIF-L@GO and vZIF-L@GO presented two Raman bands at 1345 and 1590 cm-1, and the similar intensity implied obtained composites of GO/ZIF-L showing completely vertical structure and less defects, which reflected the more coordinated growth of ZIF-L on GO. The pyrolysis of ZIF-L and GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites was clearly analyzed by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) (Figure S1d). At 300 °C, the weakly linked Hmim and water molecule were removed from the as-synthetic samples. The distinctive weight loss at about 650 °C was attributed to graphitization of GO with OCFGs participated in linker decomposition. The evaporation of Zn clusters began to dominate the weight loss with the temperature elevated to over 800 °C, which resulted from the low boiling point (907 °C) of Zn, leaving the N-rich defects.53 But the slight advantage of thermal stability (above 800 °C) of vZIF-L@GO confirmed that the weak interactions and hydrogen bonding among the vertical ZIF-Ls played a positive role for exerting synergistic effect of GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites. In addition, the adsorption properties of vZIF-L@GO were analyzed by N2 adsorption and desorption isotherms (Figure S1c). The type IV isotherm with H3 hysteresis loop indicated that the mesopores might originate from the porous ZIF-L and graphene sheets. The Brunauer‐Emmett‐Teller (BET) specific surface area showed that vZIF-L@GO (604 m2/g) has a higher surface area compared with ZIF-L@GO (517 m2/g). The wider hysteresis loop of ZIF-L@GO isotherm proved that the pore blocking might be resulted from disorder distribution of ZIF-L on GO and the accumulation of GO sheets.54
A mechanism illustrating the Cu GNC-VL formation process is summarized (Figure 1a). GO/ZIF-L sheets were reduced and transformed to Cu GNC-VL (Figure 1f and S5c) and Cu ZIF-L@GO (Figure S5a) after the carbonization treatment. The structure and active components of catalysts was clearly tracked by XRD pattern (Figure 2a). The peak of amorphous graphite-like carbon changed significantly at around 2θ = 23.6 ° or 43.2 ° representing the interplane (002) and innerplane (110) reflections of graphite carbon, respectively.55, 56 Cu GNC-VL and Cu ZIF-L@GO presented the similar characteristic peaks at 2θ = 43.07°, 50.2°, 73.7°, 89.6° and 95°, corresponding to Cu (111), Cu (200), Cu (220), Cu (311), Cu (222), respectively (JCPDS card no. 04-0836). The special diffraction peaks at 2θ = 36.3° and 61.1° were exclusively belonged to the Cu2O (111), Cu2O (220) residue existed in Cu GNC-VL, respectively (JPPDS no. 78-2076). Raman spectroscopy of the carbonizations was present in Figure S3b. The intensity ratio of the graphite-like peak (ID / IG) is related to the concentration of covalent defect sites. Hence, the relative increase of ID / IG ratio of Cu GNC-VL (1.18) revealed the abundant defects and the suppressed graphitic degree. To demonstrate the positive effects of defects derived from mild graphitization conditions, the adsorption kinetics experiments at surfaces of catalysts were characterized in Figure S6. The type III isotherm with H3 type hysteresis loop in N2 appeared an obvious difference that BET surface area of Cu GNC-VL was significantly enlarged, which might benefit from the abundant defects resulted from

the evaporation of Zn clusters during calcination and additional porosity between vertical ZIF-Ls as well as the stacking of N-doped graphene sheets, and the CO2 adsorption isotherms also confirmed that as-synthesized catalysts have a stronger force fields with carbon dioxide.
The evolution of structural properties, morphology, composition and valence state of Cu GNC-VL were investigated by electron microscopy (SEM and TEM), and Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Figure S5, SEM pictures witnessed the thermal reduction of Cu2+. During the heat treatment, Cu2+ was converted to monodisperse copper nanospheres (white spherical particles) with the polycrystalline structure. This conclusion was further demonstrated by TEM and high-resolution SEM images. Cu nanospheres were embedded in microporous N-doped porous carbon (Figure 1f). Moreover, the corresponding energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (Figure 1g) showed that N and Cu were homogeneously distributed. The high-angle annular dark-field scanning TEM (HAADF-STEM) image (Figure 1e and S7a) revealed that the as-synthesized Cu GNC-VL maintained a spatial structure, and Cu/Cu2O polycrystal presented a multi-layered
Figure 1. (a) The formation of Cu GNC-VL. (b) Surface and (c) cross-section morphology SEM image of vZIF-L@GO. (d) Corresponding SAED pattern, (e) HAADF-STEM images and (f) SEM image of Cu GNC-VL. (g) Corresponding EDS maps reveals the homogeneous distribution of Cu and N.
three-dimensional distribution. The ring-like selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) in Figure 1d, The Cu (111), Cu (220), Cu (311) and Cu2O (111) crystal plane were observed on Cu GNC-VL whereas the crystal plane of Cu2O was absent on Cu ZIF-L@GO (Figure S7b). These observations were consistent with the XRD results, indicating that the white monodisperse copper nanospheres had similar morphology but different crystal structure. XPS was further characterized the evolution of valence state and composition of elements. With the evaporation of volatile components, the highest content of N was observed on Cu GNC-VL (8.75 at%), which superior to the Cu ZIF-L@GO (5.91 at%) and pyrolyzed ZIF-L (5.09 at%) because its weak interaction between vertical ZIF-Ls
prevented the decomposition of organic linkers inside ZIF-L (Table S1). Highly porous N-doped carbons originated from the inheritance of structural-irreversible defects which derived from the massive evaporation of Zn, N, O, producing aplenty active sites. The high-resolution N 1s XPS spectra (Figure S8) was deconvoluted into three sub-peaks at 398.4, 400.4 and 401.3 eV, corresponding to pyridine-like, pyrrole-like, graphene-like nitrogen, respectively.57 The atomic concentrations of N allocated to pyridine-N, pyrrole-N, graphitic-N were 45.81%, 14,77%, 39.42% for Cu GNC-VL, respectively. The N-heteroatoms are considered as the active sites for decreasing adsorption energy of CO2 electroreduction, the promoting followed the sequence: pyridine N, pyrrole N, pyridine N.58 The total content of pyridine-like and graphenelike N of Cu GNC-VL was outmatched than that of pyrolyzed ZIF-L and Cu ZIF-L@GO, which not only laid a foundation for CO2RR to alcohols but also increased the conductivity of the catalysts. These results implied that Cu GNC-VL exerted maximumlly the synergistic effect of Cu/Cu2O-loaded vertical GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites
for its defect-abundant NPC and CO2 diffusion channels as well as a consecutive conductive network towards CO2RR.
To further determine surface composition and valence states valence states of Cu inside Cu GNC-VL, the Cu 2p XPS spectra and Cu LMM Auger spectra were measured. In Figure 2c, the peaks situated at 952.2 and 932.3 eV belonged to Cu(I)/Cu(0) species whereas the peaks observed at 954.3 and 934.5 eV should be distributed to Cu(II). It did indicate the existence of Cu oxides on the surface of Cu GNC-VL and Cu ZIF-L@GO and imply low content of Cu2+ because of the disappearing satellite peaks. 59 To distinguish the metallic Cu (0) and trace Cu (I), the high-resolution Cu Auger LMM spectrums (Figure 2b, d) of Cu ZIF-L@GO and Cu GNC-VL before and after pyrolysis were analyzed. The peaks

discovered at 572.4 and 572.48 eV can be assigned to Cu (II) before pyrolysis whereas the peaks at 569.1 and 567.88 eV should be associated with Cu (I) and Cu (0) after pyrolysis. To prove the stability of the valence state of Cu in the catalyst, Cu Auger LMM spectrums were further characterized after the optimal potential electrolysis and final electrolysis, respectively (Figure S6c, d). Though a small amount of Cu (I) was reduced to Cu (0) with the decreased binding energy of Cu from 569.1 to approximately 568.6 eV, Cu GNC-VL still maintained the composite structure of Cu/Cu2O. As for Cu ZIF-L@GO, the stability of the valence state of Cu (0) was not affected by the reduced 0.3 eV of the binding energy of Cu. Cu GNC-VL gave a broad and asymmetric peak, implying the existence of Cu(I) and Cu(0) in a stable state.60 Subsequently, the calculation of the surface composition of Cu was about 0.6% in Cu GNC-VL, and the percentage content of Cu(I) was 70.58% (Table S2).The high distribution Cu2O acted as the initiator for the dimerization of *CO, promoting the formation of C2 products. To the best of our knowledge, this catalytic behavior outperforms those of most of the reported catalysts (Table S3).
To investigate the electrochemical reduction reaction of CO2, a series of electrochemical tests were implemented on the cathode in H-type electrolytic cell. The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) (Figure 3a and 4a) exhibited a more positive onset potential for Cu GNC-VL (-0.46 V vs. RHE) than that of Cu ZIF-L@GO and pyrolyzed ZIF-L. The Cu content of Cu ZIF-L@GO (0.522%) and Cu GNC-VL (0.504%) were measured by the inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), respectively. These catalysts were measured a similar loading, but showing different catalytic activity. This result was attributed to the synergistic effect of composite crystal
Figure 3. (a) LSV curves in the CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 electrolyte with scan rate of 10 mV s−1, (b) partial ethanol current density plots, (c) electrochemical double-layer plot, (d) Nyquist plots of pyrolyzed ZIF-L, Cu ZIF-L@GO, Cu GNC-VL.
structure of Cu/Cu2O nanoparticles embedded in Cu GNC-VL and highly dispersed particle with efficient activity and uniform active sites. In Figure 3b, the partial current density of ethanol reached 8.69 mA cm-2 at -0.87 V, which was larger than that of Cu and pyrolyzed ZIF-L. In addition, the relevant partial current densities of other products listed in Figure S12
also proved that Cu GNC-VL displayed higher selectivity and charge efficiency. It could be seen that Cu GNC-VL and Cu ZIF-L@GO did exhibit excellent ability to generate hydrocarbons or alcohols and inhibit the hydrogen evolution reaction, which provided sufficient conditions for efficiently producing ethanol on Cu GNC-VL. Encouraged by the improvement of catalytic performance of CO2 electroreduction, the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) was mentioned to investigate the relevant reaction kinetics of pyrolyzed ZIF-L, Cu ZIF-L@GO and Cu GNCVL. In consideration of the fact that ECSA is positively correlated with double-layer capacitance (Cdl), the Cdl value was approved to evaluate the intrinsic activity of catalysts (Figure 3C, S9). Compared with blank carbon paper, the value of Cdl was increased by 7 times with catalyst loaded. However, the Cdl of Cu-based catalysts were about 5 times higher than that of pyrolyzed ZIF-L, demonstrating that the Cu doping did increase the intrinsic activity of catalyst. Moreover, Cu GNC-VL provided abundant electron sources to guarantee transmission of electrons because of the extra capacitance attributed to
electron absorption ability of the vertical structure and distributed Cu/Cu2O. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) (Figure 3d) was used simultaneously. The Nyquist plots revealed that a smaller semicircle diameter at low frequencies, explaining the lower interfacial chargetransfer resistance from the electrodes to electrolyte existed in Cu GNC-VL.61 To clarify the kinetic activity of CO2 electroreduction, the Tafel slope (Figure 4b and S11b) was used to reflect the possible intermediate medium determination steps of the catalytic process. Obviously, the Tafel slope of Cu GNC-VL (313 mV dec-1) was smaller than that of Cu ZIF-L@GO and pyrolyzed ZIF-L. It demonstrated that good kinetics of Cu GNC-VL might promote ethanol generation described as more efficient electron transport and

The resulting products were measured by 1H NMR with water suppression and gas chromatography (GC) (Figure S10), respectively. The internal standard, dimethyl sulfoxide and phenol, were used as reference for quantitative calculation (Figure S13). To verify the electrocatalytic performance of carbon dioxide electroreduction, we unified the electrolysis potential from -0.57 to -1.07 V vs. RHE (Figure S14a). The FE (Figure 4c, d and S11a) reflected that the maximum FEethanol of Cu GNC-VL reached 70.52% at -0.87 V vs. RHE and FEmethanol of 19.13% at -0.77 V vs. RHE. But the FEethanol decreased to 8.64% and 40.18% for pyrolyzed ZIF-L and Cu ZIF-L@GO, respectively. To prove the stability of the catalyst, the electrolysis experiment was carried out at -0.87 and -0.77V vs. RHE for 12h on Cu GNC-VL and Cu ZIFL@GO, respectively (Figure S14). The negligible decay of current densities indicated the stability of Cu GNC-VL in the test duration. It is not difficult to find that Cu GNC-VL showed the best physicochemical properties. Good conductivity and uniformly dispersed active center were the advantage of CO2RR to produce ethanol efficiently. The added two-dimensional semiconductor, GO, not only enhanced the conductivity of the catalyst, but also provided chelating sites with Zn2+ for the vertical growth of ZIF-L. However, it is clear that Cu/Cu2O composite crystal supported on N-doped porous carbon derived from the vertical ZIF-L@GO was essential for Cu GNC-VL showing excellent electrocatalytic performance compared to Cu ZIF-L@GO with similar content of Cu. The amorphous Cu/Cu2O inside Cu GNC-VL catalyst obtained by calcination, on the one hand, achieved reasonable regulation of the distribution of nanoparticles. On the other hand, the loaded nanoparticles also affected the geometric structure of porous carbon, improving the conductive performance of the catalyst. Advantageously, edge and corner sites originated from the amorphous Cu were also participated in CO2RR. The declining faraday efficiency and selectivity of ethanol also proved that Cu(111) (binds to activated CO2) and Cu2O(111) (dilutes negative 40.18% charge) sites are devoted to promotion of CO2 activation with favorable kinetics and thermodynamics, and amorphous edge and corner sites on Cu GNC-VL surfaces goosed the C−C coupling.62
 CONCLUSION
In summary, we synthesized successfully cross-like ZIF-L and vertical ZIF-L on the surface of GO. The homogenous and vertical growth of GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites exhibited excellent electrical conductivity, high active surface area, electrocatalysis stability. At -0.87 V vs RHE, Cu GNC-VL exhibited a remarkable FEethanol of 70.52%, with a considerable current density of 10.4 mA cm-2. This work took the advantage of the excellent physical and chemical properties of MOF, and exerted the synergistic effect between MOF derived NPC and GO-derived graphene. GO/ZIF-L nanocomposites with directional structure takes another small step forward converting CO2 into C2 productions.
